question:
A previously healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of blisters and redness on his neck and chest for 2 days. He has also had a fever. He is lethargic and has not eaten well since the rash appeared. He has not had coughing, wheezing, or dysuria. He is an only child and there is no family history of serious illness. His immunizations are up-to-date. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg. Examination shows flaccid blisters over his neck and trunk that rupture easily. Areas of erythematous moist skin are also noted. Twirling an eraser over the trunk results in a blister. Oropharyngeal examination is normal. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 12 g/dL
Leukocyte count 22,000/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 77%
Eosinophils 3%
Lymphocytes 18%
Monocytes 2%
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 60 mm/h
Urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"?

enhanced_information: The clinical presentation of a 4-year-old boy with flaccid blisters that rupture easily, fever, lethargy, and a positive Nikolsky sign, along with a high leukocyte count with neutrophilia, aligns with Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS). This condition is characterized by the presence of superficial blisters and erythematous skin, often without mucosal involvement, which is consistent with the normal oropharyngeal examination. The elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate supports an inflammatory process, which is typical in SSSS. The retrieved evidence paths, while broad, confirm the association of erythema and fever, which are present in this case. Other options such as Pemphigus vulgaris and Toxic epidermal necrolysis typically involve mucosal surfaces, which are not affected here, and Bullous pemphigoid is rare in children. Scarlet fever would present with a different rash pattern and often involves pharyngitis. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
